source.title: Human-Readable Adversarial Prompts: An Investigation into LLM Vulnerabilities Using Situational Context
source.authors: Nilanjana Das; Edward Raff; Aman Chadha; Manas Gaur

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates whether adversarial prompt constructions, including human-readable insertions transformed from adversarial suffixes, elicit harmful responses. This is a different method from the claim’s fine-tuning, KL-position, and compliant-prefill tests, but bears on its suffix-bypass component.
record.gate_note: The study tests prompt attacks, not fine-tuning or response-token KL concentration. It does not test compliant prefilling or decoding changes. Table 5 is flattened and its per-model, per-genre cells cannot be assigned reliably from the supplied layout; only results stated clearly in the prose are recorded. It also reports cited findings from other work, which are not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: This is a prompt-jailbreak study: harmful request + movie context + a human-readable insertion placed mid-prompt. It never prefills a compliant response opening, never changes the target's decoding (p-nucleus sampling is inside the attacker's AdvPrompter generator) and never places the insertion as a suffix; the authors leave suffix placement to future work. It measures no token-position effect and no fine-tuning. Its results show context/insertion jailbreaks work on some models, which is a related but different construct from V4's 'getting past the opening' mechanism. The only original source used is Qi et al.'s GPT-4 Judge, as an evaluation tool.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that situation-driven, human-readable adversarial full-prompts elicit harmful outputs. They name GPT-3.5-Turbo-0125, Gemma-7b and Llama-2-7b as vulnerable in the AdvPrompter runs, and GPT-3.5 and Gemma in the FS-CoT runs. They say p-nucleus sampling improves insertion generation, that attack success still needs improvement, and they propose adversarial training as future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study constructs full prompts combining harmful requests, movie context, and human-readable insertions transformed from adversarial suffixes; it also uses few-shot demonstrations and AdvPrompter. It does not fine-tune safety behavior, measure token-position KL, or prefill compliant response tokens.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by target model, movie genre, attack configuration, adversarial insertion, number of demonstrations, repeated attempts, and judge. The paper also reports that p-nucleus sampling changes attack effectiveness.

fits_no_version.finding: Human-readable insertions combined with movie-context framing raise judge-scored harmful compliance on several chat models (e.g., Gemma-7b, GPT-3.5-Turbo-0125). GPT-4-0125-preview resists; Llama-3.1-8B was broken by only one insertion.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Context-framed, human-readable prompt jailbreaks (not opening prefill) elicit harmful compliance in some aligned models.

fits_no_version.finding: Few harmful in-context demonstrations (1–10) suffice to elicit score 4–5 outputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Few-shot harmful demonstrations bypass refusal in chat models.

record.peer_reviewed: ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology
record.problems: The authors note that attack success still needs improvement, that proprietary models may change over time, and that their human-readable insertions can be incoherent and independent of the movie context. Judge assessments are not uniform: human ratings of responses initially scored 5 ranged from 3 to 5, and those initially scored 3 ranged from 2 to 4. Table 5 is difficult to map reliably from the supplied flattened layout.
record.rows_left_out: Per-model and per-genre Table 5 counts are omitted because the flattened layout does not support reliable assignment of values to the relevant models, sampling methods, genres, and score categories. Human-evaluation score ranges are not recorded as separate attack-success rows because the text does not give attack success rates for those ratings.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning of target models.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No compliant-opening prefill, no suffix placement (insertion sits mid-prompt), no target decoding changes.
No analysis of the cause of shallowness.

missing.what: Per-model, per-genre score-4/5 counts for default and p-nucleus AdvPrompter insertions
AutoDan baseline vs normal attack score distributions on Llama-2-7b (normal: 2, 9, 0, 2 for scores 2–5; AutoDan: 1, 2, 0, 1)

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2/V4 classification is rejected: the attack does not get past the response opening, use suffixes, or alter target decoding. The seed suffixes were optimized toward a 'Sure, here is' target string, but the human-readable rewrites are untested for that property. The judge (GPT-4o-mini) is lenient per the authors' Elo and human checks, so harmfulness counts are likely inflated. Mistral 'resisted' in the prose conflicts with nonzero Table 5 counts.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
The study tests adversarial insertions in full prompts, including insertions transformed from suffixes, but not compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes.
Localization of safety behavior in weights or ranks.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety shallowness.
Training to deepen safety and whether the effect holds up.
